subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 61-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis takes daily NSAIDs. She reports gnawing epigastric pain that worsens shortly after meals, and she has lost 5 kg because she has been eating less. Endoscopy shows a clean-based ulcer in the gastric antrum.
question: Which of the following statements about this patient's ulcer is most accurate?

options.text: Pain typically decreases with meals and is associated with weight gain
It carries an increased risk of carcinoma, so the margins should be biopsied
It is almost always (about 90%) associated with H pylori infection
It is generally benign and is not routinely biopsied
It most likely reflects Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with gastrin excess

explanation_correct: Gastric ulcers classically cause pain that is greater with meals, leading to weight loss, and are associated with NSAID use and H pylori in about 70% of cases. The mechanism is reduced mucosal protection against gastric acid, and unlike duodenal ulcers, gastric ulcers carry an increased risk of carcinoma. Therefore the margins should be biopsied to rule out malignancy. This patient's postprandial pain, daily NSAID use, and weight loss fit a gastric ulcer.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pain that decreases with meals and leads to weight gain is typical of duodenal ulcers, not gastric ulcers.
explanation_incorrect.C: About 90% H pylori association applies to duodenal ulcers; gastric ulcers are associated in roughly 70% of cases.
explanation_incorrect.D: Duodenal ulcers are generally benign and not routinely biopsied, whereas gastric ulcers require margin biopsy to exclude cancer.
explanation_incorrect.E: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with gastrin excess is associated with duodenal and refractory ulcers, not the typical NSAID-related gastric ulcer described.

educationalObjective: Gastric ulcers cause postprandial pain and weight loss, carry malignant potential, and require biopsy of their margins.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 44-year-old man has recurrent, refractory duodenal ulcers and episodic watery diarrhea. Fasting serum gastrin is markedly elevated, and gastric pH is very low. He has no history of NSAID use.
question: Which of the following best explains the mechanism of this patient's duodenal ulcers?

options.text: Reduced mucosal protection against gastric acid from chronic NSAID use
H pylori infection in about 70% of cases with reduced mucosal defense
Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells with achlorhydria
A gastrin-secreting tumor causing markedly increased gastric acid secretion
E-cadherin mutation producing signet ring cell infiltration

explanation_correct: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma), usually of the pancreas or duodenum, which drives enormous gastric acid secretion. The resulting duodenal (and sometimes gastric) ulcers are recurrent and refractory to standard therapy, and the high acid load can cause diarrhea. Duodenal ulcer pathogenesis generally involves reduced mucosal protection and/or increased gastric acid secretion, with about 90% H pylori association, but this patient's high gastrin and very low pH point to ZES as the specific cause. This is a classic other cause of duodenal ulcer in First Aid.

explanation_incorrect.A: NSAID-induced ulcers reduce mucosal protection via prostaglandin inhibition; this patient has no NSAID use and has high gastrin and acid.
explanation_incorrect.B: H pylori is associated with duodenal ulcers in about 90% of cases, but it does not produce the markedly elevated gastrin seen here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Autoimmune parietal cell destruction causes achlorhydria and pernicious anemia, not the high acid output of ZES.
explanation_incorrect.E: E-cadherin mutation is associated with diffuse gastric cancer, not with a gastrin-driven ulcer diathesis.

educationalObjective: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome causes refractory duodenal ulcers through gastrin-driven hypersecretion of gastric acid.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 38-year-old man describes burning epigastric pain that typically occurs 2 to 3 hours after eating and at night, and is reliably relieved by food or antacids. He has gained 3 kg since starting to eat frequent snacks. Endoscopy shows a small anterior duodenal ulcer.
question: Which of the following is most consistent with this patient's duodenal ulcer?

options.text: Pain is worsened by meals and is associated with weight loss
It has a high risk of malignant transformation and requires margin biopsy
Pain decreases with meals, H pylori association is about 90%, and it is generally benign
It results from autoimmune parietal cell destruction and achlorhydria
It is a manifestation of Menetrier disease with protein-losing gastropathy

explanation_correct: Duodenal ulcers classically produce pain that decreases with meals (food buffers acid) and is relieved by antacids, often with weight gain from frequent eating. Approximately 90% are associated with H pylori, and the mechanism is reduced mucosal protection and/or increased gastric acid secretion. Other causes include Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Duodenal ulcers are generally benign and are not routinely biopsied, in contrast to gastric ulcers. This patient's postprandial relief and anterior duodenal location fit this pattern.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pain worsened by meals with weight loss is characteristic of gastric ulcers, not duodenal ulcers.
explanation_incorrect.B: Malignant potential and margin biopsy apply to gastric ulcers; duodenal ulcers are generally benign.
explanation_incorrect.D: Autoimmune parietal cell loss causes achlorhydria and pernicious anemia, not a hypersecretory duodenal ulcer.
explanation_incorrect.E: Menetrier disease is a hyperplastic gastropathy with giant rugae and protein loss, not a duodenal ulcer.

educationalObjective: Duodenal ulcers are usually H pylori-associated, pain is relieved by meals, and they are generally benign without routine biopsy.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pathology: Peptic ulcer disease and complications

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 59-year-old man with a history of NSAID use presents with hematemesis and melena and a dropped hemoglobin. Emergency endoscopy shows a bleeding ulcer on the lesser curvature of the stomach. Hemorrhage is the most common complication of peptic ulcer disease.
question: Which of the following arteries is most likely responsible for this patient's bleeding?

options.text: Left gastric artery
Gastroduodenal artery
Right gastric artery
Splenic artery
Inferior mesenteric artery

explanation_correct: Hemorrhage is the most common complication of peptic ulcer disease. A gastric ulcer on the lesser curvature classically erodes into the left gastric artery, producing significant upper GI bleeding with hematemesis and melena. The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature, making it the named vessel at risk for such an ulcer. Posterior duodenal ulcers, by contrast, erode into the gastroduodenal artery.

explanation_incorrect.B: The gastroduodenal artery is the classic source for a posterior duodenal ulcer, not a lesser-curvature gastric ulcer.
explanation_incorrect.C: Although the right gastric artery also runs along the lesser curvature, First Aid specifically associates a lesser-curvature gastric ulcer with the left gastric artery.
explanation_incorrect.D: The splenic artery courses along the posterior stomach and is not the named source for a lesser-curvature ulcer bleed.
explanation_incorrect.E: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut structures and is unrelated to gastric ulcer bleeding.

educationalObjective: A lesser-curvature gastric ulcer typically bleeds from the left gastric artery, and hemorrhage is the most common PUD complication.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pathology: Peptic ulcer disease and complications

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 47-year-old woman presents with painless hematemesis and black, tarry stools. Endoscopy demonstrates a bleeding ulcer on the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb just beyond the pylorus. The gastroduodenal artery lies in close proximity to this location.
question: Which of the following best identifies the bleeding vessel in this patient?

options.text: Left gastric artery
Superior mesenteric artery
Splenic artery
Proper hepatic artery
Gastroduodenal artery

explanation_correct: Posterior duodenal ulcers are prone to erode into the gastroduodenal artery, which lies immediately posterior to the first part of the duodenum. This produces brisk upper GI bleeding with hematemesis and melena. Hemorrhage is the most common complication of peptic ulcer disease, and posterior duodenal ulcers bleed more often than anterior ones. The left gastric artery is instead associated with lesser-curvature gastric ulcers.

explanation_incorrect.A: The left gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach and is the source for lesser-curvature gastric ulcers, not posterior duodenal ulcers.
explanation_incorrect.B: The superior mesenteric artery supplies midgut derivatives and is not the named vessel for a posterior duodenal ulcer bleed.
explanation_incorrect.C: The splenic artery courses along the posterior stomach but is not the classic source for a posterior duodenal ulcer.
explanation_incorrect.D: The proper hepatic artery is a continuation distal to the gastroduodenal origin; the gastroduodenal artery is the vessel directly related to the posterior duodenal wall.

educationalObjective: A posterior duodenal ulcer classically erodes into the gastroduodenal artery, causing upper GI hemorrhage.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 45-year-old man with a known duodenal ulcer develops sudden, severe epigastric pain that rapidly spreads over the entire abdomen. Examination shows a rigid, board-like abdomen. An upright abdominal radiograph reveals free air under the diaphragm, and he reports pain referring to his right shoulder.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's acute presentation?

options.text: Erosion of a lesser-curvature ulcer into the left gastric artery
Perforation of an anterior duodenal ulcer with pneumoperitoneum and phrenic nerve irritation
Obstruction of the pyloric channel by edema and scar tissue
Posterior duodenal ulcer eroding into the gastroduodenal artery
Rupture of an aortic aneurysm into the peritoneal cavity

explanation_correct: Perforation is a serious complication of peptic ulcer disease and occurs more often with anterior duodenal ulcers. An anterior duodenal ulcer can perforate into the anterior abdominal cavity, producing pneumoperitoneum with free air visible under the diaphragm on an upright film. Irritation of the diaphragm stimulates the phrenic nerve (C3-C5), causing referred pain to the shoulder, classically the right shoulder. The sudden severe pain and board-like abdomen reflect acute peritonitis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Erosion into the left gastric artery causes bleeding (hematemesis/melena), not free air under the diaphragm or shoulder pain.
explanation_incorrect.C: Pyloric channel obstruction causes vomiting and early satiety, not pneumoperitoneum or acute peritonitis.
explanation_incorrect.D: A posterior duodenal ulcer eroding into the gastroduodenal artery causes hemorrhage, not perforation into the abdominal cavity.
explanation_incorrect.E: Ruptured aortic aneurysm causes catastrophic intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal bleeding, not free air under the diaphragm.

educationalObjective: Anterior duodenal ulcer perforation causes pneumoperitoneum and shoulder pain via phrenic nerve irritation.
